drills.q: In one sentence, why does freezing early layers and fine-tuning only late layers usually work well for a task close to pretraining?
drills.a: Early layers encode general, broadly reusable features that transfer directly, so only the task-specific late-layer mapping needs to be relearned.

drills.q: Name the two variables that determine where on the adaptation spectrum (frozen -> full fine-tune) you should sit.
drills.a: Dataset size and domain distance from the pretraining distribution.

drills.q: A model fine-tuned to output terse structured JSON starts giving degraded, terse answers on unrelated general chat afterward. Name the failure mode and one fix.
drills.a: Catastrophic forgetting. Fix: lower the learning rate, freeze more of the base, add rehearsal data, or switch to PEFT so the base weights never change.

drills.q: Why is a hard label a weaker training signal than a teacher's softened probability distribution in distillation?
drills.a: A hard label treats every wrong class as equally wrong. A teacher's distribution encodes real similarity structure between classes (dark knowledge) that a one-hot label discards, and that structure is extra useful signal for the student.

drills.q: Why does the distillation loss multiply the KL term by T^2 instead of using it plain?
drills.a: Softmax with temperature T shrinks gradient magnitude roughly as 1/T^2 as T increases; multiplying by T^2 corrects for that shrinkage so the soft-target term doesn't get numerically drowned out relative to the hard-label CE term.

drills.q: You need to compress a BERT-scale model as aggressively as possible while retaining close to baseline accuracy. TinyBERT beats DistilBERT's ratio — what's the mechanistic reason?
drills.a: TinyBERT uses feature-level distillation (matching intermediate hidden states and attention matrices across a two-stage general-then-task-specific process), giving a much richer per-layer training signal than DistilBERT's response-only (final logits) distillation.

drills.q: Legal flags a plan to generate training data by scraping outputs from a competitor's hosted LLM API to fine-tune your own small model. What's the real risk, concretely?
drills.a: Most frontier providers' terms of service explicitly prohibit using their outputs to train a competing model — this is a live legal issue, not theoretical, matching the substance of OpenAI's dispute with DeepSeek over alleged ToS-violating output extraction for distillation.

drills.q: Your team has 50,000 labeled examples for a new classification task and is debating distillation vs direct fine-tuning of the small target model. Which do you recommend, and why?
drills.a: Direct fine-tuning of the small model. Distillation earns its cost when your own labeled data is too thin to teach the decision boundary well; with 50,000 labeled examples you likely have enough signal already, so skip the teacher-management and licensing overhead.

drills.q: Explain why PEFT is structurally immune to catastrophic forgetting in a way full fine-tuning is not.
drills.a: PEFT freezes the base model's weights entirely and trains only a small set of added parameters (e.g. LoRA's low-rank matrices), so the original weights — and thus the base capabilities they encode — never change. The adapter can even be removed to recover exact original behavior.

drills.q: You only have API access to a frontier teacher model (no logprobs). How does your distillation approach change, and what do you lose?
drills.a: You do sequence-level distillation: generate (input, teacher-output) text pairs and supervised-fine-tune the student directly on the generated text as the target. You lose the dark-knowledge benefit, since you never see the teacher's full probability distribution over alternative tokens, only its chosen output.

drills.q: A small internal tool serving 50 requests/day is considering distilling a large fine-tuned model into a smaller one for cost savings. Is this worth it?
drills.a: Usually not. At that volume the inference-cost savings are negligible relative to the engineering cost of building and validating a distillation pipeline — ship the large model and revisit only if traffic grows enough to change the cost-benefit calculation.
